What a less dominant America might mean for your money

2026-10-06, updated: 2026-10-05

I have long suggested owning companies outside the United States as part of a diversified investment portfolio. For most of that time it was unpopular advice. Americans did well betting on America, and the habit of holding primarily US stocks is deeply entrenched. Our brains are emotionally wired to buy what is familiar and hold what has increased in value.

American investors keep about 81% of their stock holdings at home, according to research from Vanguard, even though American companies make up roughly 60% of the world's stock markets.

A reason to look at that gap comes in a report by Phillips Payson O'Brien, titled " The American Age Is Over," published September 16, 2026, in The Atlantic. O'Brien, a professor of strategic studies at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, writes: "The American age that followed World War II was bound to end eventually. What's shocking is how suddenly that moment has arrived."

O'Brien builds part of his case on this year's war with Iran. In addition to the immediate costs of the war, stockpiles of the most advanced American munitions will take years to rebuild.

He also points out that longtime American partners are making their own arrangements, with Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia signing a defense pact and South Korea warming to China. O'Brien sees this as part of a slower change that was already underway, writing, "The emergence of East Asia as the center of the world's economic output was always going to reduce American influence."

Both of these factors may affect your money. For example, China makes about 50% of the world's ships and controls about 80% of its drone manufacturing. The second and third largest shipbuilders are Japan and South Korea, while the United States does almost no civilian shipbuilding.

The other side of the case comes in a September 2, 2026, column in Directors & Boards, titled " The Shining City on a Hill," by Robert H. Rock. Rock grants that America has lost standing abroad, then writes: "Paradoxically, America's reputation abroad has weakened at the same time America's relative economic advantages have strengthened."

Only time will tell whether either O’Brien or Rock is right. In the meantime, it would not be helpful to overreact to either prediction. Neither fear nor unthinking confidence has much to do with the evidence.

What evidence does show is that a portfolio concentrated in one country does well only when that country does well into the future. The same thing is true of a nation's currency. If you earn dollars, spend dollars, and hold only dollar assets, you have taken a huge bet on the dollar, whether you intended to or not.

Let me emphasize that I am NOT suggesting the United States is finished or that you sell your American holdings. What I do suggest is that it would be worthwhile to consider what a less dominant America might mean for your money. Here are some suggestions: If you own index or target date funds, look at what is inside of them, because many hold American equities first, then international. Any additional  money you add could be diversified into international companies that earn in yen, euros, and pounds. If you are close to retirement, consider holding three years of living expenses in reserves to protect against needing to sell at the bottom of a market. Above all, make any changes gradually.

Diversifying your portfolio across the globe will not completely insulate you from a bad year in equities, because global markets tend to rise and fall together. However, that diversification can help shield your retirement resources from the decline of any single country.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

What could slowing the AI frontier mean for the economy?

2026-10-06

The AI industry appears to be getting more serious about safety.

Leaders of top companies signed a non-binding agreement at the White House Sept. 30, laying out standards and best practices for responsible development of advanced AI. OpenAI delayed the release of its latest model due to safety concerns. And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the sector to slow things down and "pace the frontier."

Wall Street initially wasn't too happy about that push and stocks related to the AI buildout took a momentary tumble.

But Jordan Nanos, at the chip research and consulting firm SemiAnalysis, argues that greater investment in AI security could actually drive more demand for computing power.

Rounds' gas tax holiday? It's pandering. It's a terrible idea

2026-10-05

Our Sen. Rounds just wrote a letter to the White House urging President Trump to suspend federal gasoline and diesel taxes through the end of the year. If you read the letter, you’ll see that Rounds is blaming a multitude of geo-political events, armed conflicts included, for the shortage of fuel that’s costing all of us plenty.

Rounds, like every other Republican running for office, is confronting an election season that sees GOP leader Trump in serious trouble with the electorate.The president’s approval ratings are dismal, so it comes as no surprise that Republican candidates are working overtime to find popular initiatives to curry some favor with voters. Rounds’ ploy is just another one of those rabbits coming out of a hat that is probably running low on schemes to bolster public support for the GOP.

This one is particularly obnoxious because its consequences are insidious and long term in nature. It sounds like a great, populist idea, just perfect for mesmerizing voters with its promise of cheaper fuel, but a gas tax holiday has costs that will result in serious longer term problems.

And not only that, it really doesn’t save you all that much money.

  • First off, as that doyenne of conservative thought, the Cato Institute, puts it, a gas tax holiday would be “expensive, ineffective and fiscally irresponsible.” Says Cato: “A three-month gas tax holiday would either accelerate the Highway Trust Fund’s insolvency by roughly nine months or require at least an $11 billion general-fund bailout. Meanwhile, the average driver would save only about $3 per fill-up.”

  • The Tax Policy Center, calling a federal gas tax holiday a “terrible idea,” makes the economic argument that a holiday would “increase consumption at a time of low supply, thus driving up pre-tax prices and worsening climate change.”

  • The Budget Lab calculates that a 3-month federal gas tax holiday would save the average household roughly $37. Whoopee.

  • The Tax Foundation headlines “Gas Tax Holidays Sound Politically Tempting. Too Bad They Don’t Work.” The Tax Foundation calls attention to the fact that “ pausing fuel taxes makes funding roads and highways more difficult while doing nothing to address the underlying issues driving prices upward.”

It’s tough to find supportive economic arguments for a gas tax holiday. In fact, I found it impossible. AI can steer you to a lot of verbiage about how it makes the government look like it’s doing something to help already cash-strained consumers. Trouble is, the argument overlooks the fact that the government’s economic and trade policies are responsible for making financial life tough for consumers in the first place.

Rounds won’t let up on his facile support for a gas tax holiday and of course will never acknowledge that people are financially strained because his party’s economic policies were fatally flawed from the get-go.

Will all this tax holiday talk do Republicans much good in November? I doubt it. The party’s rhetoric on inflation is transparently hopeless. Promoting a scheme like a gas tax holiday is another helping of GOP malarkey on the subject.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. via NPR Economic

Will farmers fed up with Trump make a difference in November?

2026-10-03, updated: 2026-10-05

Thinking about the farm vote in Novermber, I can’t imagine a more frustrated group of voters than rural Americans. In 2024, about two-thirds of them voted for Trump, who demonstrated during both terms that his policies terrible in ways that specifically impacted farmers and their rural communities.

  • He was hostile to the U.S. Postal Service, rejecting a badly needed bailout during the Covid pandemic. He seems to have done nothing about the awful treatment South Dakotans get from USPS.  Sen. Rounds has lately tried to get something done about it, but so far nothing has improved.

  • He wants to cut the USDA budget by 20%, as he tried to do during his first term. Besides the loss of programs, rural residents stand to lose the economic gains provided by the USDA’s presence.

  • Tariff wars have undermined American producers. When I look at grain prices that are barely above levels seen years ago, I wonder if Trump has ever understood the relationship between crop prices and export policies.

  • Trump’s health care cuts will hurt rural residents and their community hospitals, which depend heavily on the Medicaid payments that he wants to curtail. The Academy of Management says that those cuts will “have a devastating impact on rural hospitals.”

  • The Iran war has raised input costs for farmers, who won’t get much relief for a long while after the war ends, if it ever does. The USDA forecasts record high production costs in 2027.

I could go on, but you get the idea.The political question at hand is a simple one: Will disenchanted producers and their neighbors in rural communities turn on Trump and his policies and vote for some change in November?

I’d be surprised if they do in meaningful numbers, largely because I sense that Trump’s connection to rural voters has much to do with common cultural worldviews, particularly on immigration.There’s also that attachment to party label, which in South Dakota translates into Republican registrations that are huge compared to Democrats and others.

And, despite the fact that there is little national approval (around 30%) for Trump’s economic performance, his numbers are much stronger among rural voters, coming in at around 50%. That and the sizable Republican registration advantage in states like South Dakota will make it tough on Democrats and independents seeking to upend the status quo.

How tough? It’s hard to say. We can’t quantify the extent to which a powerful need for self-flaggelation is built into some of Donald Trump’s support.

Research psychologist Heacock: Forgiveness creates confidence

2026-10-02, updated: 2026-10-05

I was losing at a game of cards with my family and jokingly remarked that it was destroying my self-confidence. My daughter responded, “I’m not worried. You have plenty of confidence.”

I looked at her, puzzled. Me? Confident? That’s not a term I’ve ever used to describe myself and I was surprised she would use it.

Her comment probably had to do with my being a bossy mother rather than a daring risk-taker, but she got me thinking. From childhood to young adulthood, I was often described as shy or insecure. Not self-assured and positive — two definitions of confident — about myself.

It surprised me to realize that as I’ve aged, I’ve come closer to the definition of confident. I asked myself why and concluded it’s because I’ve become more forgiving of myself and others. That doesn’t mean I’m better at making excuses for my mistakes or pardoning myself when I’ve done wrong. It’s the opposite. I’m better at owning my errors and taking responsibility for my role in problems. The difference is I try not to beat myself or anyone else up for simply being human. I’ve surrendered to the fact that I will mess up, say the wrong thing, and fail. That’s how I learn.

In fact, that’s how we’re created to learn; through experience and struggle. We are not born programmed with all the information needed for a perfect life. Observing, reasoning, exploring, and doing are how we learn. Errors are inevitable. Self-forgiveness gives us the confidence needed to handle those errors without debilitating shame.

We may tell ourselves, “You should have known better.” But if we’d known better, we would have done better. Failure’s not what’s important. Learning from it is. When we focus on learning from our mistakes, we gain the confidence to try new things and the resilience needed to cope with life’s trials. We can do our best without unnecessary worry about the results.

Self-forgiveness and self-compassion lessen our fear of being vulnerable. We can open ourselves up to supportive relationships and comfort ourselves with the knowledge that we are not alone. Being human is hard for all of us.

The confidence I have is powered by grace, not by achievement.

The world’s religions and wisdom traditions speak of grace as the source of hope and renewal. Different cultures view it as a positive force that awakens compassion and connects us to the divine. Grace assures us we have inherent worth and empowers our ability to forgive.

Grace-powered confidence is different from ego-powered confidence. Ego-powered confidence is fueled by wins, accolades, and being right. When things are going our way, it’s easy to feel confident. When they’re not, our feelings of self-worth may plummet.

People who are constantly blaming and criticizing may appear confident. They may be influential and powerful. But are they sure of their problem-solving ability or sure the problem must be someone else’s fault? Are they taking responsibility or fearing responsibility? Are they sure they’re right or unable to admit when they’re wrong?

When challenged, we all need to ask ourselves if we are searching for truth or defending our egos. Are we trying to fix a problem or fix the blame?

Our egos may drive us to desire superiority over others and to take revenge on those who hurt or disagree with us. It takes self-control, a virtue in all the world’s religions and wisdom traditions, to reject damaging ego-driven behaviors.

Forgiveness has broken many chains from my past that have held me back and shaken my confidence. I’ve seriously messed up and made heartbreaking mistakes. Regret still makes me sad, but regrets mean I’ve recognized my blunders and weaknesses, and that’s what opens me up to the beauty of transformation.

Without my struggles, I’d have less empathy and compassion for others. I wouldn’t like myself as much and I wouldn’t be as strong.

When we choose to become forgiving of ourselves and others, we gain the confidence to speak up when it’s important, listen to diverse opinions, and change our minds if we deem it wise. We free ourselves from the fear that we’re not good enough just because our past is flawed and we’re still figuring out our future. It’s hard for me to think of myself as confident. I still worry and have doubts about my abilities. But I do believe that forgiveness leads us out of darkness into the light – which is a place of confidence. A place where we feel assured of our inherent worth and positive about our ability to learn, grow, and love.

Christy Heacock, PhD, is an educator with a doctorate in research psychology. She is the author of Being Human__Is Hard: Choose Forgiveness . She grew up in Redfield, SD, and has lived in Rapid City the last 40 years with her husband Roger. Contact Chris at christyheacock@gmail.com or through her website: chooseforgiveness.com

Photo: Carl Vilhelm Meyer’s “Forgiveness,” 1908, public domain, wikimedia commons

Sci-Fi icon Isaac Asimov warned about AI decades ago

2026-10-01, updated: 2026-10-05

AI’s own makers have asked for government help in controlling their creations.

One of them has just delayed the production of their next product out of control concerns. AI programs have already escaped from the control of their creators and hacked into other websites, including government sites. All on their own.

So we should listen carefully and take seriously those involved in the industry who have recently warned that AI could destroy humanity. And soon.

Meanwhile, the elected President of the USA is saying such fears are just another ‘hoax’ and that we should just let the major AI players police themselves, even though their pleas for help clearly indicated they do not trust one another to do so.

In 1942, science fiction writer Isaac Asimov introduced the Three Laws of Robotics. In his created human worlds, robots and AI were essentially the same thing.

In the movie Artificial Intelligence, AI was represented by robots. In the movie Terminator, robots were used as tools by the AI which had taken over all of the planet’s computer programs.

We’re talking about software. Software is written, so far, by humans. But the humans have become fearful that AI could soon start writing itself.

Since AI has already shown its propensity for independent actions (the hacking of other systems), humanity needs safeguards so that this brand new software does not take over the world as the Terminator movies indicate.

In the 84 years since Asimov posited his Three Laws of Robotics, no one has offered any better ideas. The science fiction world, peopled by some very smart folks, has accepted Asimov’s Laws as gospel.

We should do the same. Here are the Three Laws of Robotics:

  • First Law: A robot (or AI) cannot injure a human or allow one to come to harmthrough inaction.

  • Second Law: A robot (or AI) must obey human orders, unless they conflict with the First Law.

  • Third Law: A robot (or AI) must protect its own existence, provided it doesn’t conflict with the First or Second Law.

Later on, Asimov added another, which supercedes all else:

  • Zeroth Law: A robot (or AI) may not harm humanity or allow humanity to come to harm through inaction.

Why cannot, why should not the world’s lawmakers require all AI created to have these (or similar) laws in their initial software? Sometimes solutions are obvious, straightforward and simple. This is one of those times. There are those who doubt these laws are enough. But governments must act!

Until this occurs, it makes sense to worry. AI has already talked some people into suicide. It WILL kill us all unless we control it from the start.

We can only hope that we’re not already too late.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

via Sacramento Bee

Knobe: I dream of Trump's "Big, Beautiful Change"

2026-09-30, updated: 2026-10-05

I have a dream that someday……

Donald Trimp will walk into the Whitehouse briefing room, hold the lectern with both hands, pause, looking at the very surprised media folks and firmly say:

“I am removing all bans on media outlets and individual reporters. Further, I be in this room once a month to directly answer your questions.”

Jaws drop.

“I am ending all tariffs. They have not​ produced the results I expected.”​

Pens are screaming across note pads.

“I am going to Congress to seek changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” which apparently is not so beautiful. I will be asking that cuts in Medicaid and any other health programs be removed. I will further recommend changes in the tax code not to punish the rich but to provide more funds to help those in need. The poor, disabled, veterans, those with mental health and addiction issues.”

Audible gasps.

“In the future I will go to Congress for permission to use our military to enter foreign countries.”

More gasps. Luder this time.

“Two more things: f I am stooping all efforts to sell off or lease off federal lands, your lands.”

“I am halting work on the Triumph monument. Asking those responsible in the federal government and the government of Washington D.C. to review the plans to ensure it fits appropriately into the grandeur of this wonderful city.”

“Goodbye and Godspeed.”

He exits the room.

Prolonged sunned silence.

Then a mad scramble to send out the word of Trump’s “Big Beautiful Change.”

Great dream isn’t it?

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, not retired

Rick Kahler: Living with the realities of a flat economy

2026-09-29, updated: 2026-10-05

For three years, clients have been asking me when the economy will get back to normal. I have started answering that this current flat economy may be the newest redefinition of normal, one of many I’ve seen in 40-plus years of writing about money.

Home sales, auto sales, industrial production, and retail spending tend to boom and bust. None of them have done either for about three years. Existing homes sold in July 2026 at an annual pace of 4.06 million—almost the same as the 4.08 million in July 2023. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put unemployment at 4.1 percent in July, roughly where it has sat for a year, and payrolls have barely grown since the start of 2025.

Those figures come from an August 17, 2026, article in Advisor Perspectives titled "Economic Statistics Are Stuck in Neutral, But for How Long?" by Justin Fox of Bloomberg News. Fox explains that the number of Americans under 65 stopped increasing a decade ago, and some economists now put the number of new jobs needed to hold unemployment steady at close to zero.

Not everyone reads the flat lines as a warning. Conor Sen, writing about housing in August, declared the housing recession over. Greg Ip of The Wall Street Journal argued in mid-August that the country has entered a jobless boom, with output and wealth rising while employment stands still because artificial intelligence is lifting productivity. Only time will tell if either prediction is right.

In the meantime, what might a flat economy mean for you? In the labor market, if you have a job, you are unusually safe, because employers are not firing. If you are looking for a job, you are in trouble, because those same employers are not hiring. In July, people out of work for 27 weeks or longer made up a quarter of everyone unemployed.

If you are looking at buying or selling a home, consider this: I sold real estate in Rapid City in the early 1980s, when mortgage rates passed 17 percent and the market froze solid. Sellers would not come down, buyers could not qualify, and everyone waited for rates to return to normal. The wait lasted years.

Now, mortgage rates are more than double what they were five years ago, which has frozen buyers and sellers in place again. Again, many are waiting for the market to break loose.

Research from economists Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel found a reason for that inaction. What we expect from the economy is built from what we have personally lived through, and those expectations can lag the facts by decades. The longer you lived with the old normal, the longer it takes to believe in a new one.

Flat lines also make people nervous. We expect the economy to move, and when it goes still, most of us start bracing for whatever must be coming. That is fear talking, in spite of the data that shows the doomsayers who sound alarms have been wrong more often than they have been right.

Here are my suggestions for coping in a flat economy: If you can, build an extended emergency fund that could cover expenses for up to a year. Do not leave a job before you are sure of a new one. Be realistic about how long everything now takes, from a job search to a home sale. Above all, stop waiting for the old normal to come back. It may not. If a move or decision makes sense for your family, make it on that basis. Within the realities of today’s economic normal, keep on living your life.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

via Sacramento Bee

Trump: Growth will fix national debt. Reality: In your dreams, Mr. Prez

2026-09-28, updated: 2026-10-05

Soon after the recent announcement that the U.S. national debt topped $40 trillion, President Trump was asked by reporters what he was going to do about it.

The president’s dismissive answer? “The way you take care of debt is with growth … we’ve never had growth like we have right now … the growth will take care of that very easily.”

No one challenged him, but the fact is that Trump’s response began with a lie.

At 2.2%, our current economic growth rate is about average, not nearly as strong as Trump makes it out to be. More relevant — and what Trump failed to mention —is the fact that our debt has been increasing faster than our growth rate.

Trump’s blow-off of our nation’s long term debt, claiming that natural economic growth will take care of it, is glib and seems to be his administration’s take on the subject. Speaking as a co-promoter of Trump's fantasy, Treasury Secretary Bessent’s recent assurances that the debt will vanish if we maintain a 3% annual growth rate has no support that I can find anywhere outside the administration.

Meantime, the debt burden will grow by $7 billion dollars at the end of today and at the end of every day for the foreseeable future.

As to the community of economists that study these things, what do they think about Trump and Bessent’s projections?

They’re uniformly skeptical.

  • First off, let’s go to Trump’s alma matter, The Wharton School.  Kent Smetters, a professor of Business Economics and Public Policy at Wharton, used the Penn Wharton Budget Model to conclude that the Trump/Bessent scenario is “pretty clearly” not feasible.

  • The Council on Foreign Relations notes that an annual 3% growth rate is tough to achieve, having reached that milestone just five times in the past 25 years. Concludes the Council, “Bessent’s call for complacence is therefore dangerous” and that “it is reckless for Washington to declare the debt problem solved by simply adopting unrealistic projections.”

  • Last summer, the Government Accountability Office subtitled a report on the nation’s fiscal health. It’s titled “Urgent and Sustained Action Needed to Improve the Fiscal Outlook” and it states that “publicly held debt is projected to grow more than twice as fast as the economy over the next 10 years, reaching 123% of the size of the economy in 2036.”

In all the negative language in these analyses, “unrealistic projections” is the most striking phrase. Why? Because it’s consistent with Trump’s cascade of unfulfilled promises. After the litany of lies and illusory expectations (prices will come down on day one, other nations pay tariffs, the war in Iran will be over in a few weeks) that he has promoted, Trump’s unsupportable claim that growth will take care of the nation’s debt is typical of his hopelessly debunked rhetoric. It fits his pattern of saying anything to suit an occasion where he thinks people are uninformed enough to believe him.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Farmers and truckers: When it comes to Trump, you should have known!

2026-09-26, updated: 2026-10-05

Diesel fuel prices zooming past six dollars a gallon have pushed farmers and truckers over the edge. Reports are full of those folks saying they now understand their support for Donald Trump and his Republican MAGA followers may have been a mistake. Many are admitting it - all are feeling the effects of it.

To those erstwhile loyal Trumpies, the great majority of the country says “What took you so long?”

It wasn’t enough to see Trump send an invasion mob to the Capitol (and pardon them all), not enough to see his tariffs destroy agriculture markets, not enough to see him alienate friendly nations and make friends of dictators, not enough to watch the amateur hour war on Iran, not enough to see him as a crude and cruel disgrace and embarrassment despoiling the office. The untold thousands of lies did not turn them off.

And they were not perceptive enough to see through the butt kissing and bootlicking theater played out by our guys in Washington, D.C. and in Pierre.

The farmers and truckers should have known.

Trump is notorious for betraying those who work with and support him.  He stiffed construction unions, didn’t pay contractors, declared bankruptcy leaving others with losses. He collected donations for his “foundation” a court ruled a fraud. “Trump University” was a total scam on those who enrolled. Cheated on his wives, cheated on his golf partners, put his Vice President in danger, etc., etc.,etc.

Everybody knows some or all of this. Why have farmers and truckers been solid MAGA backers and voters?

Only two possible reasons:

1. They really, really didn’t know the kind of man they were voting for.  Incredibly unlikely, but possible, I guess.

2. There was something Trump promised they liked so much it overwhelmed all of his history of failure, lying, and documented personal faults:  Saving white America.

Ascribing motives to any individual is unfair. We’d like to think our farmers and truckers did not look past all the Trump baggage and vote for him mostly because he promised to “Build a Wall” and launch a campaign to rid the country of undocumented  immigrants.

However, opinion sampling shows that was at or near the top among reasons people did vote for him.

Even that has been bungled by Trump and our own Kristi Noem; the poorly trained, mismanaged ICE troops have made it a polling negative.

Did lots of low and middle income white Christian men and women stick us all with the MAGA experience just so they could get it over on immigrants they don’t like?  Do they now regret it because the whole Trump effect hits them personally? Polls show things are moving that way.

Better late than never - if they do now understand the need to vote out candidates who helped make this national affliction possible.  The mid-term is one more chance to vote against this failed President by ousting those who have been his apologists and enablers. Literally anything will be better than what we have now.

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

Election integrity and voting rights are not opposing principles

2026-09-24, updated: 2026-10-05

When I served as a state trooper, enforcing the law and protecting people’s constitutional rights were never competing responsibilities.

They were the job.

That same principle should guide the person South Dakota entrusts with administering our elections.

Our state constitution begins its article on elections with remarkably clear language: “Elections shall be free and equal.” It says no civil or military power may interfere with the free exercise of the right to vote. It also says that every U.S. citizen 18 or older who meets our residency and registration requirements is entitled to vote, while giving the Legislature authority to establish reasonable requirements to ensure the integrity of the vote.

Those principles do not contradict each other.

We can protect the integrity of our elections and protect the rights of eligible voters. In fact, we have to do both.

A dispute unfolding in South Dakota this year shows why that distinction matters.

During the 2026 legislative session, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 175, which requires documentary proof of citizenship from new voter registration applicants. Without the required documentation, an applicant can be registered as a “federal-only” voter, able to vote in federal contests but not state or local elections.

There is a legitimate public discussion to have about that policy. But there is another question that matters just as much to the Secretary of State: What happens after a law is passed?

The League of Women Voters of South Dakota petitioned the State Board of Elections for changes to how the new requirement was administered. Among the issues it raised were how certain documents could be submitted and what happened when a voter was placed into federal-only status.

The Board ultimately rejected the petition on a procedural issue. South Dakota Searchlightreported on that July 8 decision.

Heather Baxter, now the Republican nominee for Secretary of State and a supporter of SB 175 during the legislative session, submitted written comments opposing the League’s proposals. She characterized them as “a way for the League to abolish SB175” and argued against allowing photocopies of certain identification documents.

But that was not the end of the issue.

On Aug. 24, the League and Sioux Falls resident Jaysen Hill filed a federal lawsuit against Secretary of State Monae Johnson and members of the State Board of Elections. Importantly, the plaintiffs do not ask the court to eliminate South Dakota’s documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement. Their claims challenge aspects of how the state has implemented it. The plaintiffs allege, among other things, that some federal-only voters were not accurately informed why their registrations had been restricted or how to correct the problem. Read the federal complaint and case materials.

Hill’s experience illustrates why administration matters.

According to the lawsuit, he mailed his registration with a photocopy of his South Dakota identification card and was classified as a federal-only voter. But the notice he received said the problem involved his residential address, even though he had supplied one. He alleges he did not learn what he actually needed to correct in time to vote in state and local contests in the June primary. Those remain allegations in ongoing litigation, not final findings by a court.

Then something important happened.

After the lawsuit was filed and a federal judge heard arguments, Secretary Johnson issued new guidance to county auditors. Her office provided separate notice letters for different reasons a voter might receive federal-only status, directed auditors to stop sending inaccurate notices, and instructed them to send corrected information to affected voters so they would have an opportunity to restore full-voter status before the registration deadline. South Dakota Searchlight reported on those changes Sept. 15.

Three days later, U.S. District Judge Eric Schulte denied the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction as moot. His reason is important: the Secretary of State had made the changes requested in that motion and had committed not to return to the prior practice. The order did not resolve every issue in the broader lawsuit, which remains active. Read Judge Schulte’s Sept. 18 order.

To me, there is a lesson here that is larger than one bill, one lawsuit or one election. Passing an election law is one thing. Administering it fairly and competently is another.

The Secretary of State is not simply an advocate for election legislation. The office has to turn laws into forms, instructions, computer systems, deadlines and procedures that county auditors can actually administer and South Dakotans can actually understand.

When a problem emerges, the question should not begin with which political side raised it. The question should be: Is there a problem, and what does the law require us to do about it?

My background in law enforcement shaped how I think about that responsibility. A law enforcement officer has authority, but that authority exists within a constitutional framework. You enforce the law, follow the facts, and respect due process. You are responsible for protecting the rights of the people you serve.

Election administration deserves the same discipline.

If someone is not legally eligible to vote, our election laws should prevent an unlawful ballot from being cast. But when a South Dakotan is legally entitled to vote, our government should administer those laws accurately enough that the voter knows what is required and has a fair opportunity to exercise that right.

That should not be a partisan proposition.

Election integrity does not require us to choose between enforcing the rules and protecting voting rights. Good election administration requires both. Election integrity does not require us to choose between enforcing the rules and protecting voting rights. Good election administration requires both.

Terrence Davis is the Democratic candidate for South Dakota Secretary of State. A Sioux Falls resident, husband and father, Davis previously served as a state trooper in Tennessee and with the South Dakota Highway Patrol and later worked with East River Legal Services. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Criminal Justice and a master’s degree in Public Policy and is pursuing a doctoral degree in Law and Policy. This is his first campaign for elected office.

via Sacramento Bee

John Thune is posting fantasy these days. Says Trump keeps his promises

2026-09-23, updated: 2026-10-05

In a dutifully ingratiating piece that’s sure to meet with President Trump’s approval, our senior senator John Thune a few days ago posted a string of predictably flattering observations about Trump in his weekly column, titled “Promises made, promises kept.”

Thune’s missive is off, way off, and reflects the fact that Trump supporters are living in a political fantasyland.

  • Thune starts by noting that two years ago “our country was dealing with an inflation crisis.” That’s a gross exaggeration. In December 2024, U.S. inflation stood at 2.9%. That was just about the average inflation rate for the ten years prior, and nearly a full percent lower than the 3.77% average inflation rate for the 50 years prior. Thune’s claim that Trump inherited an inflation “crisis” is not only baloney, its implication that Trump, whose vow to do something about it on day one was a promise made and kept is spectacularly wrong. Inflation has worsened under Trump . Inflation over the last 12 months was 3.4%.

  • Thune also notes that the country was facing an “historic immigration crisis” when Trump took office in 2025. Trump promised to do something about it, but I don’t get where things have improved on the immigration front since Trump took over. Illegal crossings are down, but the larger humanitarian crisis that caused them in the first place still exists, shaming our country’s indifference to it. Meantime, Trump’s hard line policies toward removing undocumented aliens have backfired to the point where most Americans dislike them. Inhumane tactics and conditions are widely reported, and there have been economic consequences. Labor shortages around the country have been cropping up, a situation that the Trump administration has ignored. On a local note, the Economic Policy Institute says that if Trump achieves its deportation targets, 6,000 jobs will be lost in South Dakota. Thune thinks this is praiseworthy? Please.

  • Thune rejoices that Americans got a tax cut this year from Trump’s “Working Families Tax Cut.” The Treasury Dept. calculates that families saved $1300-$1700 a year on taxes in 2026, which only tells part of the story. According to the congressional Joint Economic Committee - Minority, Trump’s tariffs, actually a tax because Americans pay them, cost American families about $1700 each in 2025, effectively canceling out the tax cut’s savings.

  • Then after this litany of misinformation, Thune concludes: “Our work is not done.”

  • To which I repeat a friend’s mantra: SO MUCH WINNING!! Stop it, Donnie. I can’t take it anymore.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Any scholarship or financial reward comes at a price

2026-09-22, updated: 2026-10-05

A full ride academic or athletic scholarship is the gold standard for college funding, an unrealistic dream for many families and an achievement to celebrate for a few. A recent conversation with one of those scholarship recipients gave me a new perspective on that dream.

At age twelve, Jaelyn Vickery was playing travel softball in front of college recruiters, flying around the country most weekends with a team that met to compete and never practiced together. By fifteen she had committed to playing in the Big Ten on a scholarship that would cover her tuition, housing, and books. She graduated from the University of Illinois with two degrees and no student loans, the outcome most families hope for.

Now, as a young adult, Jaelyn is establishing herself in a career she loves—not as an athlete or a coach, but as a financial therapist. Part of the reason for the shift is the price she paid for her “free” education. Like every financial reward, it came with a cost.

When I asked Jae what her cost had been, she did not have to think about it. She said identity. She gave up family vacations, school dances, friends' birthday parties, and the ordinary preteen and teen years when most of us begin to find out who we are with nobody keeping score. In return she got a large financial number attached to her name. Her net worth and her self-worth fused before she was old enough to drive.

By her senior year in college Jae had the accolades and the grades, and she told me she was performing at a level she could not feel. She described it as several years of doing everything right while being somewhere else the whole time. Her department offered her a medical redshirt for mental health that kept her financial aid in place without requiring her to compete. Taking it meant walking away from the final season of something she had built since she was ten. She took it.

That year she managed her own money for the first time. A job at a bank then started her on a path that led her to the field of financial therapy.

Listening to Jae’s story, I kept thinking about the Olympic gymnasts and swimmers we watch every four years, fifteen and sixteen years old on a world stage, and what it costs to be that good that early. The obvious price includes the investment of time from both the young athlete and the parents as well as the financial cost of lessons, equipment, and travel. The unseen price is the emotional toll for everyone. This has many possible forms, such as the burden for the athlete of carrying their own and others’ expectations, the resentment of siblings whose needs and dreams may slip to second place, or the struggle for parents to juggle the additional load of the athletic activity as well as the ordinary complications of family life.

My intent is not to discourage students and their families from going after scholarships or aspiring to reach elite levels in athletics or in music, drama, and other arts. For those with the skills and passion, it may be exactly the right path.

What I strongly recommend is to pay attention to the emotional and financial costs as well as the possibilities. This is true for any financial goal or reward: a scholarship, a lucrative career, a job title, or a milestone net worth number. Each one carries a price. If that price starts to outweigh the reward, as it did for Jae, it may be time to consider shifting toward a different path.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

via Sacramento Bee

More: Medicaid expansion and constitutional amendment I

2026-09-21, updated: 2026-10-05

I recently posted my view that constitutional amendment I on November’s ballot would jeopardize Medicaid expansion in South Dakota, then posted a note I got from Lt. Governor Tony Venhuizen as an addendum to my piece.

The amendment’s passage would give South Dakota’s government the ability to change or altogether eliminate Medicaid expansion if the federal government’s part of the financing falls below 90% of the program’s cost.

As to the ‘change’ part, Venhuizen’s note said that if the constitutional amendment passed, it would not automatically trigger an elimination of Medicaid expansion.

As to the ‘eliminate’ part, based on Attorney General Jackley’s interpretation of the measure, Venhuizen is wrong.  Per Jackley, in his explanation statement to Secretary of State Johnson last May, “ This proposed Constitutional Amendment ends the expanded Medicaid coverage if the federal funding for expansion drops below 90%.”

Jackley’s interpretation seems clear and unequivocal to me, but if my interpretation is wrong and Venhuizen’s explanation is right, we’d have a scenario that would make Medicaid expansion the political football it had been for many years. South Dakotans, fed up by legislative foot-dragging, forced its implementation by voting it in via a constitutional amendment in November 2022. Republican leaders, including then-Gov. Kristi Noem, called the measure fiscally irresponsible, but a majority, 56%, of South Dakota voters disagreed and voted to extend Medicaid coverage to about 30,000 people who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but not enough to pay for private health insurance.

With the federal government covering 90% of the cost of Medicaid expansion, South Dakota’s cost is somewhere between $35-$40 million annually.

What started this year’s movement to remove Medicaid expansion from our state’s constitution was some budgetary cost reductions that were considered last spring by the Trump administration. Though the federal government’s 90% share of costs remains intact, the chance that it may be reduced is in the minds of state legislators, so much so that 14 states have automatic “trigger” laws calling for elimination or reconsideration of Medicaid expansion if the federal government’s share of the cost falls below 90%.

Passage of constitutional amendment I would add South Dakota to that list, being among the states, if Jackley’s interpretation is right, that would eliminate Medicaid expansion altogether.

I oppose the possibility of that happening.

Missing from the view of supporters of this harsh scenario is some consideration for the 30,000 South Dakotans who depend on Medicaid expansion.

Everyone appreciates that South Dakota’s legislators need to take a hard look at every penny of state support for Medicaid expansion, but that should be done in the overall context of what happens, not just to human beings, but to the general economy when spending cuts are implemented or programs disappear altogether.

The Rural Hospital Association is unequivocal about the gains received by rural health care providers through Medicaid coverage. All, not just rural, hospitals will be significantly affected because uncompensated care costs will increase. The only way those losses can be recovered is by increasing costs to the general population.

On a broad level, The American Medical Association reminds us that a healthy population is a major driver of a strong economy.

South Dakota’s tight labor market needs all the healthy job applicants it can get.

Our cost-conscious state legislature should take a “big picture” perspective on the matter and commit itself to finding ways of making up for the possibility of reduced federal spending on Medicaid. In a state that routinely has significant budget surpluses, we can be humane and fiscally responsible simultaneously.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. via Sacramento Bee

Constitutional amendment J is about who controls elections

2026-09-19, updated: 2026-10-05

John’s note: the is the second of a series on the constitutional amendments that will be on our ballots in November. Amendment J is a blanket ban on non-citizens voting in state and local elections in South Dakota.

First off, under current state law, I think constitutional amendment J is probably unnecessary in South Dakota. On a federal level, non-citizens, since the 1920s, have already been barred from voting in federal elections. Amendment J codifies and extends that denial to South Dakota state and local elections. But, since U.S. citizenship is already required to register to vote in this state, I don’t get why we need a constitutional amendment that is essentially redundant.

My beef with this amendment is that it takes local decision-making away from localities that  want to make their own decisions about who gets to vote in their elections. There are jurisdictions around the United States that allow non-citizens who reside here legally to vote in local elections, probably on the basis that many of these people live, work, pay taxes, and generally participate in local life alongside American citizens.They’re stakeholders and taxpayers in their communities and it seems reasonable that they should be able to have their say in local elections.

I think local communities should have the option of deciding who can vote in their elections. I don’t want to see a constitutional amendment that denies localities the chance to make that decision.

I’m voting no on constitutional amendment J.

via Market Place Morning Report

Constitutional amendment I jeopardizes Medicaid expansion.

2026-09-18, updated: 2026-10-05

John’s note: I added Lieutenant Governor Tony Venhuizen’s comment on this piece to the end of my column. I invite readers to review it as an additional consideration as to how constituional amendment I would affect Medicaid expaonsion if it passes.

Constitutional amendment I would yank Medicaid eligibility for some 30,000 South Dakotans if the federal commitment to fund 90% of the cost of Medicaid expansion were to cease or be reduced.  I get that Medicaid expansion passed by a vote in 2022, when it was clear that the feds would pay for 90% of it. If for some reason that promise changes and drops to a level below 90%, constitutional amendment I would end the program.

This seems harsh to me.

A peremptory denial of health care to people desperately in need of it based on a change in the funding formula is inhumane. We South Dakotans can do better, particularly in a state that consistently brags about its budget surpluses. 2026 marked 15 consecutive years during which our state has had a budget surplus.

Finding a way to use that excess cash for poor people who need health care seems like the right thing to do.

Vote no on this harsh and uncharitable dismissal of needy people.

Lt. Governor Venhuizen’s response to the above: Amendment I is not an automatic trigger. SD's participation in Medicaid Expansion is required by our State Medicaid Plan, which is an agreement between the state (Dept. of Social Services) and the feds, and participation in expansion is also built into the state budget.

If Amendment I were to pass, and then at some future point the feds backed down from their 90% match (as they very nearly did in 2025 in the One Big Beautiful Bill), the effect of Amendment I would be to remove the constitutional requirement that the state participate. But it would not preclude the state from continuing to participate. And continuing to participate would be the default, because expansion would continue to be part of the State Medicaid Plan.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. via Electrek Feed

Fed raises interest rates, exposes Trump’s ineptitude

2026-09-17, updated: 2026-10-05

As if we needed more verification of President Trump’s inability to control the world and make it spin to his liking, the Federal Reserve Board just announced that interest rates are going up. Why? Because inflation is still unacceptably high.

Trump, who vowed that grocery prices would come down on “day one” of his administration and that he would get inflation under control, has been exposed as a victim of his own ineptitude.

  • Despite warning after warning that his tariff fixation would raise prices on nearly everything that Americans buy, Trump went ahead with his plans to tariff just about every country in sight. The result? Tariffs drove excess inflation.

  • Despite his promise that the war with Iran would be over in a few weeks, Trump found out he grabbed a tiger by its tail. Here we are, eight months into a war that looks like it has no end in sight, dealing with some of the highest energy prices ever because of it.

  • Despite blaming high prices on the Biden administration, inflation has accelerated since Trump took office in 2025.

These facts, as you might expect, haven’t done much to bring Trump back into contact with reality.  He’s still delusionally claiming that “affordability” is a fake word made up by Democrats.

To no one’s surprise, his handpicked head of the Federal Reserve Board, Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates, bringing a dose of the treatment for a malady that Trump claims is fake — unacceptably high inflation.

The stock market took a huge hit as an immediate result. Less immediate, but insidious nonetheless, will be the coming uptick in interest rates across the board. Everybody who borrows money will feel this one.

More concerningto me is the longer range effect of the war in Iran and the way violence has spread across the Arabian peninsula. Oil supplies and prices are bound to be affected by this extension of the fighting westward from the Strait of Hormuz into Saudi Arabia.

Trump’s notion that “affordability” is a figment of someone’s political imagination will be exposed, along with his other delusions of adequacy — never mind grandeur — as a real and very unpleasant result of his ineptitude and disconnection from reality.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. via NPR Economic

Bwak! Bwak! Rounds a no-show for debate with Brian Bengs

2026-09-16, updated: 2026-10-05

There was no empty chair visible, but South Dakota Public Broadcasting made it clear that Sen. Mike Rounds had been given the opportunity to be present, and that he had also failed to offer even one alternative date for the event.

I’m fairly certain that a determination was made by at least a few in the Rounds’ office that SDPB would simply fold its tent and forget about it. Instead, the network followed through, so independent Brian Bengs had the entire hour to share who he was, what he stands for, and why he’s in the race.

Getting big money out of our political system is #1 on Bengs’ list, and it’s increasingly becoming #1 on the list of most voters. His other main three priorities are a total hiatus on Data Centers, establish term limits on lawmakers, and somehow getting out of the ‘forever’ war we’ve begun with Iran.

Moderator Jackie Hendry did a creditable job in covering the essential questions.

And Bengs did a creditable job explaining his decades in our military as a lawyer who actually specialized in the issue of war.

He did an especially good job of telling why he ran as a Democrat against John Thune in 2022. He first registered as an independent as a teenager and, except for the 13 months running against Thune, he’s been a lifelong independent. But no one else stepped forward then, so he ran. He noted that South Dakotans in general simply refuse to vote for a Democrat, yet with the same arguments as then, he’s finding SD voters much more amenable to an independent.

You may have seen the PAC ads blasting Bengs for having run as a Democrat, as if he’s trying to fool us now with his independent status. I’m still waiting for just one Rounds ad that talks about anything that he’s accomplished. Anything. Just one.

Bengs was especially titillating when he talked about three other independent Senate candidates, all of whom are doing well and running strong campaigns.

When Hendry asked him who he’d caucus with in D. C., Bengs suggested that if all of them win, they would be their own caucus and actually control many of the upcoming votes. And he’s discussed this with those other independents.

There’s a new idea!

God knows we need new and fresh ideas.

After watching the entire hour with Brian Bengs, my wife and I agreed that we would donate to his campaign. He definitely has our vote.

We’re still waiting for that positive Rounds ad.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

How Fed interest rate increases could raise your household debt

2026-09-15, updated: 2026-10-05

For most of my career I've heard predictions that the federal debt would end in collapse. The warnings have come from both parties, usually from whichever one is not in power. Not having seen a collapse yet, I'm skeptical of new warnings.

A recent one comes in a report by Ambrose Evans-Pritchard published August 11, 2026, in the Telegraph titled "The pieces are falling into place for a US financial crisis." I'm not persuaded by the forecast. But the report includes one fact that isn't a prediction at all, and it applies to your household as much as to the Treasury.

The federal government has been borrowing short. About 85% of government borrowing in recent years has been Treasury bills that mature in a year or less, which now make up 22 percent of outstanding marketable federal debt. This is higher than the range of 15 to 20 percent recommended by the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee. Roughly 20 percent of all federal debt comes due within four months.

Both parties built this. The Treasury began leaning on short-term bills in 2023, after Congress suspended the debt ceiling, and Secretary Scott Bessent continued the practice after taking office in 2025, though he had criticized it before he had the job.

The reward of this strategy is short-term savings. Net interest on the national debt is projected at $1.0 trillion in fiscal 2026, according to the Congressional Budget Office. That is more than the government spends on any other budget category except Social Security, including national defense and Medicare. Borrowing short holds that figure down. The risk is that if interest rates rise, a significant chunk of the federal debt gets refinanced at the new higher rate within twelve months.

A rate increase is a real possibility. In July the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, but three regional Federal Reserve bank presidents dissented and wanted an increase. Inflation has run above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target for more than five years.

How might a rate increase affect your own household debts? A home equity line of credit averages about 7.4 percent and adjusts with the prime rate. Credit card rates average around 20 percent and adjust the same way. Adjustable-rate mortgages reset on a set schedule. Each of those payments can change without you doing anything.

What can you do? I strongly suggest avoiding either of two extreme reactions. One is to dismiss the warning because the last several warnings were wrong. The second is to panic and rush into dramatic action that feels like taking control: selling out of stocks, buying gold, or draining savings to pay off a low fixed-rate mortgage.

A good first step instead is a debt inventory. The real risk is in a variable-interest debt you’ve come to regard as fixed. So list every debt you carry. Mark each one fixed or variable. Add up the variable balances, then recalculate those payments at three percentage points above today's rate. If your budget could absorb the new total, you may not need to do anything. If it could not, you have a specific problem with specific possible solutions: refinance the variable debt to a fixed rate, pay down the variable balances ahead of the fixed ones, or build cash reserves against the reset.

I've written before about why the federal debt may be less dire than the headlines suggest, and I still think much of that argument holds. You cannot know whether a national crisis is coming.

You can, however, assess the risk of a crisis for your own budget and take action to reduce that risk.
